newsitem.title: UK: Palladium bumps on three-year low, may head lower.
newsitem.headline: Palladium bumps on three-year low, may head lower.

text.p: For the past three London fixings palladium has been set at its lowest level since September 14, 1993 and dealers see little prospect of it rising near term.
Palladium has been fixed at $116.25 per ounce twice on Tuesday and already on Wednesday morning, the lowest number since it was at $115.75 over three years ago.
Even that floor could be threatened in a market where sell orders far outweigh buys.
"I couldn't even give you a floor," one dealer said. "When there is just no supporting factor it could go where it likes."
The rest of the precious metals have been weak as well. Gold fixed at $380.80 per ounce, having been stuck under $385.00 since early last month, while silver was barely above $5.00.
Palladium's sister metal platinum at $383.75, was only $2.25 above its lowest fixing since January 28 1994 which was struck on October 1.

According to Johnson Matthey, the world's largest refiner of platinum group metals, Russia supplied about 4.2 million ounces or just over 65 percent of world palladium in 1995 and South Africa 1.6 million ounces (24.8 percent).
Dealers said palladium was caught between oversupply and low consumer demand. Speculator interest has been virtually non existent since last year.
"It has the feel of steady Russian selling. There still might be some fund stuff around but the consistency (of the selling) suggests its the Russians," another dealer said.
"The funds just lump it out," he added.
At the same time as Russian exports have been rolling out, imports by major consumer Japan have slumped compared with 1995, reflecting low activity in the key electronics sector.

Japan's palladium imports in August fell 16.5 percent from a year earlier, and imports for the first eight months of 1996 totalled 54.93 tonnes in 1996 compared with 68.01 tonnes in the same period last year.
"Japanese demand has been pretty sick this year. There are high stock levels in Tokyo," one dealers said.
Another dealer said, "The Japanese end users are only doing their (supply) contract obligations this year."

Palladium's main end uses are in electronics for its high conductivity, as part of the catalyst which cleans up car exhausts in the automotive industry, in dental alloys and a wide variety of chemical industry applications.
In 1995 electrical uses of palladium accounted for 42.6 percent of total use, followed by autocatalysts with 27.8 percent and dentistry on 20.9 percent, according to Johnson Matthey.
One reason for Russian sales into Europe was the slump of the yen against the dollar, meaning even a low dollar price was attractive compared to a weak yen, dealers said.
The possibility of speculators or investment funds riding to palladium's rescue were pretty limited, they said.
"Speculators are looking for an investment opportunity not just a bargain," one dealer said.
Furthermore when the funds did think they saw a gap in supply last year their buying rapidly raised palladium prices to $178.25 the year's high in April.
But by year-end, increased Russian supplies had helped reduce the palladium price to under $130.00 per ounce.
"All that happened was the producers increased supply. Now the specs know that if they want to sell, the producers will not be there to buy the metal back," a dealer said.
